questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A child has an abdominal lymphoma whose cells show a translocation placing MYC next to the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus. Which mechanism activates the oncogene here?
options: Point mutation of the coding sequence
Translocation placing MYC under a strong constitutive promoter, so it is overexpressed
questions.concept: Burkitt lymphoma carries t(8;14), and the same oncogene can be activated by different mechanisms in different tumours, amplification of MYCN in neuroblastoma being the classic amplification example.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry 32e, Ch. Cancer: An Overview

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Why does retinoblastoma occur earlier and bilaterally in the inherited form than in the sporadic form?
options: The inherited form involves an oncogene requiring one mutation
One RB1 allele is already mutated in every cell, so a single further somatic hit suffices
The inherited form has faster cell division
questions.concept: This is the Knudson two-hit hypothesis, and because tumour suppressor loss is recessive at the cellular level, the second hit is what determines tumour onset.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry 32e, Ch. Cancer: An Overview

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A patient with chronic myeloid leukaemia has the Philadelphia chromosome. Which fusion protein results and which drug targets it?
options: BCR-ABL, a constitutively active tyrosine kinase inhibited by imatinib
PML-RARA, targeted by all-trans retinoic acid
questions.concept: The t(9;22) fusion drives unregulated proliferation independent of growth factor signalling, and its selective inhibition is the founding example of targeted molecular therapy.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry 32e, Ch. Cancer: An Overview

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which receptor, when amplified in breast cancer, predicts response to a specific monoclonal antibody?
options: Oestrogen receptor, predicting response to trastuzumab
Progesterone receptor, predicting response to imatinib
Epidermal growth factor receptor, predicting response to tamoxifen
questions.concept: Amplification is tested by immunohistochemistry with fluorescence in situ hybridisation confirmation, and the same tumour is also assessed for hormone receptors because those predict response to endocrine therapy instead.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry 32e, Ch. Cancer: An Overview

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: How does the retinoblastoma protein normally restrain the cell cycle, and how is that restraint lifted?
options: It binds and sequesters E2F transcription factors until cyclin-dependent kinase phosphorylation releases them at the G1 to S checkpoint
It blocks DNA polymerase at the S phase
questions.concept: Cyclin D with CDK4 and CDK6 drives that phosphorylation, which is why cyclin D amplification, CDK4 mutation and loss of the inhibitor p16 all mimic loss of the protein itself.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry 32e, Ch. Cancer: An Overview

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A family has early colorectal and endometrial cancers, and the tumours show microsatellite instability. Which repair pathway is defective?
options: Nucleotide excision repair, as in xeroderma pigmentosum
DNA mismatch repair, involving MLH1 or MSH2
questions.concept: Lynch syndrome tumours accumulate errors at repetitive sequences because slipped strands go uncorrected, and this same instability also predicts response to immune checkpoint inhibition.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry 32e, Ch. Cancer: An Overview

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which tumour marker is most useful in monitoring a treated epithelial ovarian carcinoma?
questions.concept: It is unsuitable for screening because it rises in endometriosis, pregnancy, cirrhosis and peritoneal inflammation, so its real value is in following a known cancer during and after treatment.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry 32e, Ch. Cancer: An Overview

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which class of enzymes allows a carcinoma to breach the basement membrane and invade stroma?
questions.concept: Invasion also requires loss of E-cadherin-mediated adhesion and increased integrin-mediated motility, so degradation of the extracellular matrix is only one step of the metastatic cascade.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry 32e, Ch. Cancer: An Overview

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Carbohydrate chemistry, glycogen metabolism & HMP shunt
questions.stem: A child has hepatomegaly, fasting hypoglycaemia and a limit dextrin accumulating in liver and muscle. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.concept: Because only the outer chains can be removed, glycogen with short outer branches accumulates, and the hypoglycaemia is milder than in von Gierke disease since gluconeogenesis remains intact.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Metabolism of Carbohydrates

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Carbohydrate chemistry, glycogen metabolism & HMP shunt
questions.stem: A neonate has cirrhosis with an abnormal glycogen resembling amylopectin with very long unbranched chains. Which enzyme is deficient and what is the prognosis?
options: Branching enzyme deficiency, Andersen disease, which is usually fatal in early childhood
Debranching enzyme deficiency, which is mild
Acid maltase deficiency, which spares the liver
Phosphorylase kinase deficiency, which is benign
questions.concept: The abnormal polysaccharide is poorly soluble and provokes a foreign-body reaction in tissue, so the disease is one of structural glycogen abnormality rather than of impaired glucose release.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Metabolism of Carbohydrates

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Carbohydrate chemistry, glycogen metabolism & HMP shunt
questions.stem: Which activated nucleotide sugar donates glucose residues during glycogen synthesis?
questions.concept: Glycogen synthase transfers glucose from UDP-glucose to the growing alpha-1,4 chain, and glycogenin serves as the protein primer on which the first residues are laid down.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Metabolism of Carbohydrates

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Carbohydrate chemistry, glycogen metabolism & HMP shunt
questions.stem: Which enzyme of the hexose monophosphate shunt requires thiamine pyrophosphate, and how is this used clinically?
options: Transketolase, whose erythrocyte activity assesses thiamine status
questions.concept: Activation of the enzyme by adding thiamine pyrophosphate in vitro gives the activity coefficient, a rise indicating deficiency, and the same vitamin is a cofactor for pyruvate and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Metabolism of Carbohydrates

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Carbohydrate chemistry, glycogen metabolism & HMP shunt
questions.stem: Which process explains the formation of glycated haemoglobin in a diabetic patient?
options: Non-enzymatic attachment of glucose to the terminal valine of the beta chain
questions.concept: Because the reaction is non-enzymatic and irreversible over the life of the red cell, the level reflects average glycaemia over roughly 8 to 12 weeks and is falsely low when red cell survival is shortened.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Metabolism of Carbohydrates

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Carbohydrate chemistry, glycogen metabolism & HMP shunt
questions.stem: A young man has a persistently positive urine reducing sugar test with normal blood glucose, no symptoms and no treatment needed. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.concept: Fructose accumulates and is excreted harmlessly, whereas aldolase B deficiency traps fructose-1-phosphate and sequesters phosphate, producing hypoglycaemia, vomiting and liver failure after fructose ingestion.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Metabolism of Carbohydrates

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Carbohydrate chemistry, glycogen metabolism & HMP shunt
questions.stem: Which linkages form the linear chains and the branch points of glycogen?
options: Alpha-1,4 in the chains and alpha-1,6 at the branch points
Beta-1,4 in the chains and beta-1,6 at branches
Alpha-1,6 in the chains and alpha-1,4 at branches
questions.concept: Branching every 8 to 10 residues multiplies the non-reducing ends available to phosphorylase, which is what allows rapid mobilisation of glucose from the polymer.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Metabolism of Carbohydrates

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Carbohydrate chemistry, glycogen metabolism & HMP shunt
questions.stem: Which pathway explains cataract and neuropathy developing in poorly controlled diabetes through osmotic injury?
options: The polyol pathway, in which aldose reductase converts glucose to sorbitol
questions.concept: Sorbitol is trapped intracellularly because the tissues lack sorbitol dehydrogenase, drawing in water osmotically, and the reaction also consumes NADPH which weakens glutathione-dependent antioxidant defence.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Metabolism of Carbohydrates

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: How does a pure non-competitive inhibitor alter the kinetic constants of an enzyme?
options: Vmax falls while Km is unchanged
Vmax is unchanged while Km rises
questions.concept: The inhibitor binds a site distinct from the active site so substrate cannot outcompete it, whereas a competitive inhibitor raises the apparent Km and can be overcome by more substrate.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Enzymology

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: What advantage does the Lineweaver-Burk double reciprocal plot offer over the direct Michaelis-Menten curve?
options: It gives a straight line so Vmax and Km can be read from the intercepts
It removes the need for substrate measurement
questions.concept: The intercept on the y axis gives 1 over Vmax and that on the x axis gives minus 1 over Km, and the pattern of intersecting lines is what distinguishes competitive from non-competitive inhibition.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Enzymology

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Allopurinol is described as a suicide inhibitor of xanthine oxidase. What does this mean?
options: It binds reversibly at an allosteric site
It is converted by the enzyme into a product that then inactivates the enzyme irreversibly
It competes with the substrate but dissociates rapidly
It denatures the enzyme by altering pH
questions.concept: Oxypurinol formed by the enzyme remains tightly bound, so the inhibition is mechanism-based, and aspirin acting on cyclooxygenase by acetylation is the other standard example of irreversible inactivation.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Enzymology

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A patient treated for myocardial infarction develops fresh chest pain on day 4. Which marker best identifies reinfarction and why?
options: Troponin I, because it stays raised for 10 days
CK-MB, because its shorter half-life allows a new rise to be detected against a falling baseline
Lactate dehydrogenase, because it peaks late
Myoglobin, because it is cardiac specific
questions.concept: Troponin remains the most sensitive and specific marker for the initial diagnosis, but because it is still elevated on day 4 a further rise is hard to interpret, so the marker that has already normalised is more informative.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Enzymology

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A raised serum angiotensin-converting enzyme level supports which diagnosis?
questions.concept: The enzyme is produced by the epithelioid cells of granulomas so it broadly reflects granuloma burden, but it is neither sensitive nor specific enough to diagnose or exclude the disease on its own.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Enzymology

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: What is the relationship between an apoenzyme, a cofactor and a holoenzyme?
options: The apoenzyme is the inactive protein, and with its cofactor it forms the catalytically active holoenzyme
The holoenzyme is the protein alone
The cofactor is the protein part
The apoenzyme is the active form
questions.concept: Tightly bound organic cofactors are called prosthetic groups, as with haem in catalase, whereas loosely associated ones such as NAD act as cosubstrates and are regenerated elsewhere.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Enzymology

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which mechanism of enzyme regulation acts within seconds and is reversed by a phosphatase?
questions.concept: Glycogen phosphorylase and glycogen synthase are reciprocally controlled this way by the cyclic AMP cascade, which is how a hormonal signal at the cell surface is amplified into a rapid metabolic switch.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Enzymology

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A patient remains apnoeic for hours after suxamethonium during anaesthesia. Which enzyme abnormality explains this and how is it assessed?
options: Deficiency of plasma pseudocholinesterase, assessed by the dibucaine number
Deficiency of acetylcholinesterase at the endplate
questions.concept: The dibucaine number reports the quality rather than the quantity of the enzyme, so it distinguishes an inherited atypical variant from an acquired reduction due to liver disease, malnutrition or pregnancy.
questions.reference: Vasudevan Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students 9e, Ch. Enzymology

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which blotting technique is used to detect a specific DNA sequence?
questions.concept: The mnemonic follows the target, with Northern for RNA and Western for protein, and all three depend on separation by electrophoresis, transfer to a membrane and detection with a labelled probe or antibody.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry 32e, Ch. Molecular Genetics and Recombinant DNA

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which technique confirms a positive HIV screening test by detecting antibodies against specific viral proteins?
questions.concept: Viral proteins separated by size are probed with the patient serum, so the pattern of bands rather than a single signal is what distinguishes a true positive from the cross-reactivity that causes false positive screening results.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry 32e, Ch. Molecular Genetics and Recombinant DNA

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which modification of the polymerase chain reaction allows an RNA virus such as hepatitis C to be detected?
options: Nested PCR using two primer pairs
Reverse transcription PCR, in which RNA is first copied into complementary DNA
Multiplex PCR using several primer pairs
Real-time PCR with a fluorescent probe
questions.concept: Taq polymerase cannot use RNA as a template, so reverse transcriptase must generate complementary DNA first, and combining this with real-time detection gives the quantitative viral load used to monitor treatment.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry 32e, Ch. Molecular Genetics and Recombinant DNA

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which principle underlies Sanger dideoxy sequencing?
options: Chain termination by incorporation of a dideoxynucleotide lacking the 3-prime hydroxyl group
Cleavage of DNA at specific bases by chemical reagents
Hybridisation to an array of oligonucleotides
questions.concept: The absent hydroxyl group prevents formation of the next phosphodiester bond, so a nested set of fragments of differing length is produced and their separation reveals the sequence.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry 32e, Ch. Molecular Genetics and Recombinant DNA

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: How does attenuation regulate the tryptophan operon in addition to repression?
options: Ribosome stalling at tryptophan codons in the leader sequence alters formation of a terminator hairpin, so transcription stops when tryptophan is plentiful
The repressor binds the operator only when tryptophan is absent
The promoter is methylated when tryptophan is high
The messenger RNA is degraded by a specific nuclease
questions.concept: This second layer of control couples transcription to the actual charging of transfer RNA, giving a graded response, and it contrasts with the lac operon which is inducible rather than repressible.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry 32e, Ch. Molecular Genetics and Recombinant DNA

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which technique detects a submicroscopic chromosomal deletion such as that of 22q11 in DiGeorge syndrome?
options: Fluorescence in situ hybridisation with a locus-specific probe
questions.concept: Standard karyotyping resolves only changes of several megabases, whereas a labelled probe to the critical region shows a signal on one chromosome and none on the other, and chromosomal microarray gives a genome-wide equivalent.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry 32e, Ch. Molecular Genetics and Recombinant DNA

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: How does a microRNA regulate gene expression?
options: It binds the promoter to block transcription initiation
It base-pairs with the 3-prime untranslated region of a target messenger RNA, causing translational repression or degradation
It methylates histones at the target locus
It is translated into a small regulatory peptide
questions.concept: Because a single species can regulate many transcripts, loss or overexpression of one microRNA can shift a whole programme, which is why some act functionally as oncogenes and others as tumour suppressors.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry 32e, Ch. Molecular Genetics and Recombinant DNA

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Why is sodium dodecyl sulphate included when separating proteins by polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis?
options: It denatures the proteins and confers uniform negative charge so migration depends on size
It cross-links the proteins into complexes
It maintains the native folded structure
questions.concept: Migration therefore estimates molecular weight against standards, whereas isoelectric focusing separates by charge instead and combining the two gives the two-dimensional maps used in proteomics.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry 32e, Ch. Molecular Genetics and Recombinant DNA
